desc:
A directed graph has n = graph.length nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. The list graph[i] contains the nodes that node i points to (the targets of the outgoing edges of i). A node with no outgoing edges is a terminal node.

A token starts on some node and keeps moving along outgoing edges, choosing any edge it likes at each step, until it reaches a terminal node (it stops there). A node is safe if every possible way of moving the token from that node is guaranteed to end in a terminal node after finitely many steps. In particular a terminal node is safe, and a node from which the token could circle forever is not safe.

Return all safe nodes in increasing order.

graph = [[1,2],[2,3],[5],[0],[5],[],[]] -> [2,4,5,6]
graph = [[1,2,3,4],[1,2],[3,4],[0,4],[]] -> [4]
graph = [[],[0],[1]]                    -> [0,1,2]
constraints: The total number of edges is at most 8,000
graph[i] contains distinct values in [0, n - 1]; it may contain i itself (a self-loop)
hints: A node is unsafe exactly when the token can wander into a cycle from it. What does that say about the nodes that are safe, in terms of the nodes they point to?
A node is safe if all of its targets are safe (a terminal node has no targets, so it is vacuously safe). This is a 'peeling' process that starts from the terminal nodes.

Reverse every edge and run Kahn's algorithm: use the out-degree of each node as its counter, start with the terminal nodes, and whenever a node is confirmed safe decrease the counter of every node that points to it. A node whose counter reaches 0 is safe. Finally sort the safe nodes.
editorial: Call a node safe if all of its paths end. A terminal node is safe. A non-terminal node is safe exactly when each of its targets is safe: if one target is unsafe the token can go there and loop forever, and if all are safe every route ends. So safety can be discovered by repeatedly peeling off nodes whose targets are all known to be safe.

Implement the peeling with a reversed graph. For each edge i → j record i in rev[j], and let remaining[i] be the out-degree of i. Put all terminal nodes (remaining 0) in a queue. When a node j is popped it is safe: for each i in rev[j] decrease remaining[i], and when it hits 0 every target of i is safe, so i is safe too and joins the queue.

Nodes on a cycle, or with a path into a cycle, never reach 0, so they are never reported. The result is sorted before returning. A DFS with three colours (unvisited, in progress, done) is an alternative, but the reversed Kahn approach avoids deep recursion. Time and space are O(n + m) apart from the final sort.
